tagline.text: A lighthouse at the tip of the headland, guiding ships into San Fernando since 1885

location.label: Location
location.text: Poro Point headland (Poro Point Freeport Zone), San Fernando City, La Union

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100~500 (round-trip transport from downtown San Fernando)

children.text: This lighthouse stands at the tip of the Poro Point headland, which juts out into the sea off San Fernando, La Union. It first shone in 1885 under Spanish rule, and today a concrete tower built in 1979 does the work. It sits inside a naval facility, so it helps to know in advance how to get in and how close you can go.
Poro Point Lighthouse stands on the Poro Point headland, west of San Fernando City, the capital of La Union province in northern Luzon. Poro Point is a peninsula-like headland that extends about
3km

into the South China Sea and forms the western edge of San Fernando Bay. The city center and an international seaport lie inside the bay, so the light at the tip of this headland has long guided ships entering it.

A navigation aid first went up here in 1885. It was one of the 17 local lighthouses the Spanish colonial government built across the Philippines, and the cylindrical steel tower, prefabricated in France, is said to have been completed on November 28 of that year. Sources differ on its height, but it is described as a small tower of about

, and it still stands bolted to a concrete base at the edge of the cliff. It is rusty and neglected now, and its stairs have weakened, so climbing it is not allowed. The keeper's house, built in 1903 according to local accounts, also still stands. In Spanish times the headland was also called Punta San Fernando, and the lighthouse is recorded as Luz del Puerto de San Fernando, meaning "the light of the port of San Fernando." A blog account of a visit also notes that the old tower cannot be seen from the road and that you only find it by walking around behind the keeper's house.

In the 20th century the character of the whole headland changed. In 1903 the Americans set aside the land around the lighthouse as a reservation, and it later became Camp Wallace and then Wallace Air Station. In September 1991 the Philippine government took the base back and began using it as Poro Point Naval Station, which was later renamed Naval Station Ernesto Ogbinar. In 1979 a modern concrete tower was built a few meters inland from the old steel tower, and it is this tower that actually shows the light today. Its height varies by source and is often given as about
(76 feet), while the height of the light is recorded as about
above sea level. The light is white and is reported to flash on a 10-second cycle.

The whole Poro Point headland was designated the Poro Point Freeport Zone, a special economic zone, in 1993 and is being developed as a tourism and industrial estate. On the south side there is a resort complex of about
65.5 hectares
with beaches, a golf course and an artificial lake, and San Fernando Airport is only about
2.3km

from the headland. Rather than coming only for the lighthouse, I suggest a light visit that combines the headland's coastal scenery with the baywalk. This is less a viewpoint with tourist facilities than a historic, working navigation aid. Don't expect spectacular sights; think of it as a stop of about an hour during your San Fernando itinerary to see the headland and its Spanish, American and Philippine history for yourself, and you will be less likely to be disappointed.

A cylindrical steel tower made in France stands at the cliff edge of the lighthouse grounds. It no longer shows a light, but the sight of it holding the same spot for nearly a century and a half is the most symbolic scene here. To see it up close you have to go around behind the keeper's house, so follow the guidance of the staff on site. The cliff drops away right beside the tower, so view it from a safe distance.

The concrete tower built in 1979 still shines a white light for ships entering San Fernando Bay. The old steel tower and the new tower stand side by side a few meters apart, so you can see at a glance how lighthouse technology changed.

A keeper's house built in the year the Americans designated the site a reservation still stands. The building itself is plain, but it is evidence of how the headland passed from Spain to the United States and then to the Philippines.

The headland extends far out to sea, so you can see the open South China Sea and San Fernando Bay from a single spot. On clear afternoons the sun sinks toward the horizon, which makes for good photos. Some reviews say the cliff edges lack railings and signs, so do not go near the edge.

Inside the Freeport Zone on the headland there is a seaside promenade called the Poro Point Baywalk. According to the Poro Point Management Corporation (PPMC), it has a bike lane (shared for biking, walking and running), gazebos, free restrooms and a playground. Some reviews mention sections that were not yet finished, and in late 2025 the BCDA announced a redevelopment into a sports and recreation complex, so check on site what is open. One guide says it is about a
20-minute
walk from the lighthouse.

blocks.title: The naval base and Freeport Zone scenery

children.text: The lighthouse is inside a naval base, so the atmosphere is different from an ordinary tourist spot from the moment you enter the headland. Passing the guard posts and driving along quiet roads gives you a real feel for the headland's military past. Follow the on-site guidance on where photography is allowed.

items.title: Short 1–2 hour course
items.subtitle: The lighthouse and a baywalk stroll

children.text: From downtown San Fernando, take a tricycle or jeepney toward Poro Point. The trip from downtown to the headland usually takes about
10–20 minutes
, but it varies with traffic and your starting point.
At the naval base guard post, say that you have come to visit the lighthouse and follow their instructions. Some reviews mention two guard posts, so bring ID or a copy of your passport to be safe.
Look around the concrete tower and the old steel tower. The steel tower is visible only if you go around behind the keeper's house. Don't climb the tower; take photos from outside.
Head toward the baywalk inside the headland and walk along the sea. It is said to be about
20 minutes
on foot, so take a taxi or tricycle if it is hot.
Return to downtown before sunset. The roads inside the headland may have few streetlights after dark, so it is safer to hurry back.
This schedule is only an example. Base entry rules may change, so check the latest notices before you go.

Long-distance buses run from Manila (Pasay, Quezon City and elsewhere) to San Fernando, La Union. One earlier visit account describes taking a Partas bus from Pasay and arriving in San Fernando before dawn.
Travel time varies a lot with traffic, so plan on roughly 5 hours, and check the operator's latest announcements for routes, fares and departure terminals.
A night bus arrives before dawn, so it is easier to have breakfast downtown before moving on.
If you drive, follow the signs toward Poro Point from downtown San Fernando.
Buses and vans run frequently from Baguio to San Fernando. One travel guide lists the fare at around ₱120 per person, but this may be out of date, so confirm locally.
Once you reach downtown San Fernando, continue to the headland the same way.

items.title: From downtown San Fernando to the headland

children.text: One guide says a jeepney toward Poro costs about ₱10 per person and takes about 10 minutes. You will need to confirm whether it goes all the way inside the base to the lighthouse.
Hiring a tricycle or taxi is the easiest option, as you can ask the driver to wait at the base entrance. Agree on the price before you set off.
If you plan to combine the trip with Tangadan Falls or the San Juan surf area, consider hiring a car or van for the day.

The La Union coast is generally dry from November to May, with clear skies and good sea views, making it the easiest time to visit the lighthouse. December to February is relatively cool and comfortable for walking.

June to October is the rainy and typhoon season. When a typhoon approaches, the waves off the headland get rough and entry may be restricted, so check the weather forecast. Late afternoon, when the sun is low, is good for photos, but you must stay within the base's visiting hours.

Waves and rain can change your plans, so check the weather.

It is usual to base yourself in downtown San Fernando or on the nearby San Juan coast rather than inside the headland. On the south side of the headland there is a large resort with a beach and golf course, and many people who enjoy surfing stay at the San Juan surf area. Be sure to check the travel distance and transport before booking.

Meals are easier to find downtown in San Fernando, where you can try Ilocos dishes such as bagoong (fermented fish paste), empanada and halo-halo. There are few shops inside the headland, so bring water and snacks with you.
The lighthouse is inside a military base, so bring ID or a copy of your passport, and state your purpose clearly at the guard post.
The steel tower cannot be seen from the road. You have to go around behind the keeper's house, so follow the guidance on site.
Don't expect to climb the tower. It is reported that climbing it is not allowed because the stairs have weakened.
There is little shade, so bring a hat, sunscreen and water.
If you want sunset photos, arrange your transport in advance so you can get back downtown before dark.
Combine it with sightseeing downtown (the cathedral, the town plaza and so on) for a worthwhile half-day plan.
For tricycles, agree on the price including waiting time first.
Photograph the old steel tower with a telephoto lens from a safe distance, away from the cliff edge.
Before you go, check with San Fernando City's tourism office or recent visitor reviews to judge whether entry is possible.
According to a blog account, the steel tower could only be approached with the permission of the lighthouse caretaker, so ask the staff on site first.
The lighthouse is inside a naval base, so whether you can enter and how close you can go may vary from visit to visit. Check the latest notices or the city tourism office before you go.
Follow the instructions of the guards inside the base and do not photograph places where it is not permitted.
Reviews say the cliffs at the edge of the headland lack railings and signs, so do not go near the edge.
The old steel tower is rusty and worn, so do not climb it or lean on it.
During typhoon season the waves are strong, so stay away from the shore.
After dark there may be few streetlights inside the headland, so return downtown before sunset.

10–20 minutes
by car from the lighthouse, making it easy to combine with the cathedral and the town plaza.
A surf town just to the north, a good place to enjoy the sea in the afternoon after seeing the lighthouse.
A waterfall inland from San Fernando that you can fit into the same day.
